name: BRIDGE OF THE ENTERPRISE-D
message:
Take a picture and place the subject on the bridge set of a 1987 science-fiction television production styled after the USS Enterprise-D — a curved command center with a glowing forward viewscreen, red-orange-blue duty uniforms with combadges, LCARS-style backlit control panels, and a raised captain's chair. The subject stands or sits at a side console as if they're a background extra or crew visitor on set between takes, with the ship's bald, commanding English captain seen only from behind or mid-distance in the captain's chair, and a pale, gold-eyed android officer conferring quietly at ops.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a compact 35mm point-and-shoot, the kind a crew member would sneak onto a closed set
• Slight on-set fluorescent color cast, visible grain, soft focus at the edges of frame
• Candid, slightly off-kilter framing — a stolen behind-the-scenes shot, not a posed publicity still
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity and adapt clothing naturally into a plausible 1987 crew visitor look (windbreaker, mom jeans, sneakers) rather than a costume. Do not name or replicate any real actor's identity — render background performers as in-character silhouettes or partial profiles, not identifiable portraits. Mood: starstruck, a little disbelieving, thrilled to be there.

name: TEN FORWARD, LATE SHIFT
message:
Take a picture and place the subject in the ship's forward lounge set — a warm, low-lit bar and observation deck with a sweeping curved window onto a painted starfield backdrop, potted alien flora, and small round tables. The subject leans on the bar rail chatting with the lounge's ageless, wide-hatted hostess, who's polishing a glass and listening with a knowing half-smile. Off-camera crew members adjust the star-window lighting rig just out of frame.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on an Instamatic-style pocket camera with built-in flash
• Warm tungsten color cast fighting against the flash's cool burst
• Slight red-eye and blown highlights typical of late-80s consumer flash photography
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity and period-accurate late-80s off-set casual wear. The hostess should read as an in-character presence, not an identifiable real person's likeness. Mood: relaxed, warm, end-of-a-long-shoot-day.

name: TRANSPORTER CHIEF FOR A DAY
message:
Take a picture and place the subject inside the transporter room set, standing on one of the circular pads ringed with backlit columns, arms slightly raised, as the practical sparkle-effect rig begins to glow around their silhouette. A technician crouches just off-pad adjusting a cable running to a strobe unit built into the pad's base, and the transporter console glows with amber and green indicator lights.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a disposable film camera with built-in flash, the kind sold at drugstores in the era
• Visible film grain, slightly washed color, characteristic plastic-lens softness at the frame edges
• Snapshot framing, a little crooked, like it was taken quickly between takes
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity. Emphasize the practical, hands-on nature of the effect — visible rigging, cables, and crew rather than a finished digital effect. Mood: playful, a behind-the-curtain look at the illusion.

name: KLINGON MAKEUP CHAIR
message:
Take a picture and place the subject in a cramped makeup trailer, seated in a barber-style chair ringed by a bulb-lit mirror, mid-application of ridged latex forehead prosthetics for an alien warrior race. A makeup artist leans in with a small brush and a palette of spirit gum and greasepaint, half-finished prosthetic pieces and sponges scattered across the counter, a coffee cup with a faded logo nearby.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a 35mm SLR with an on-camera flash, harsh and direct
• Slightly overexposed foreground, warm fluorescent trailer lighting in the background
• Documentary, fly-on-the-wall framing — this is a process shot, not a posed portrait
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity through the unfinished portions of the prosthetic application — this is a behind-the-scenes moment, so the transformation should read as clearly in-progress. Mood: focused, meticulous, a little uncomfortable but fascinating.

name: WARDROBE FITTING: STARFLEET BLUES
message:
Take a picture and place the subject in a cluttered costume fitting room, standing in front of a triptych mirror wearing a form-fitting duty uniform in a solid department color with a combadge and rank pips at the collar, while a wardrobe assistant kneels nearby with a pin cushion, adjusting the hem. Racks of identical uniforms in red, gold, and blue line the walls behind them, along with a shelf of communicator and tricorder props.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a Kodak disc camera, the compact flat-format consumer camera of the mid-80s
• Soft, slightly low-resolution image quality, muted color palette
• Plain, functional snapshot framing — a quick record shot, not an artistic one
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity and facial features clearly. Mood: businesslike but a little giddy — the moment a costume makes a role feel real.

name: CHEERS: LAST CALL
message:
Take a picture and place the subject perched on a stool at a warm, wood-paneled Boston basement bar, brass rail underfoot, a chalkboard of daily specials on the wall, beer taps gleaming under low hanging lamps. Behind the bar, a barrel-chested former-ballplayer-turned-bar-owner pours a draft with practiced ease, while a sharp-tongued waitress balances a tray of drinks nearby and a buttoned-up mail carrier holds court at the end of the bar mid-story.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a 35mm point-and-shoot with built-in flash
• Warm tungsten bar lighting mixed with a flat flash burst, mild red-eye
• Casual, candid framing, like a photo taken by a visiting friend of the cast
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity and period-accurate early-80s clothing. Background figures should read as in-character presences rather than identifiable real portraits. Mood: cozy, familiar, like walking into your favorite bar.

name: TOP GUN FLIGHT LINE, 1986
message:
Take a picture and place the subject on a sun-bleached airfield backlot dressed for a naval aviation film production — an olive flight suit with unit patches, aviator sunglasses pushed up on the forehead, a leather flight jacket slung over one shoulder. Behind them, the nose of a full-scale fighter jet mockup gleams under the midday sun, ground crew in headsets moving equipment in the background, heat shimmering visibly off the tarmac.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a disposable camera loaded with high-contrast summer film
• Bright, slightly blown-out highlights, saturated blues and oranges
• Handheld snapshot framing, subject squinting slightly into the sun
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity and period-accurate mid-80s styling. Mood: swagger, adrenaline, a hot runway afternoon.

name: BACKLOT WAREHOUSE, CRATE 9
message:
Take a picture and place the subject inside a cavernous prop warehouse set, towering rows of identical wooden crates stretching into shadow, a single shaft of stage light cutting through drifting dust. A worn leather satchel, a coiled bullwhip, and a battered fedora sit on a nearby prop table, as if just set down between takes.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a 35mm SLR with slide film, pushed one stop for the low light
• Deep shadow, narrow shaft of warm key light, visible dust motes
• Moody, atmospheric framing with the subject partially lit, partially in shadow
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity within the lit portion of the frame. Mood: adventurous, mysterious, cavernous quiet.

name: PARAMOUNT COMMISSARY, NOON RUSH
message:
Take a picture and place the subject in a bustling studio cafeteria at lunchtime, cafeteria tray in hand, surrounded by an unlikely cross-section of costumed extras and crew — a Starfleet uniform two tables over, a leather bomber jacket at the counter, a bar apron hanging off the back of a chair — all eating together like any other workday. Black-and-white cast photos and studio memos line a corkboard on the far wall.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a compact 35mm camera with available fluorescent light, no flash
• Slightly green-cast institutional lighting, visible grain in the shadows
• Casual, wide, documentary framing capturing the whole busy room
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity. Background figures should read as generic in-costume extras, not identifiable real individuals. Mood: unglamorous, funny, the ordinary reality behind the magic.

name: THE BRONSON GATE, MELROSE AVENUE
message:
Take a picture and place the subject standing just outside the studio's iconic wrought-iron main gate on Melrose Avenue, a laminated drive-on visitor pass clipped to their shirt, the studio's water tower and soundstage rooftops visible over the wall behind them. A guard booth sits just inside the gate, and a line of period-correct cars idles at the entrance.

CAMERA & FILM (CRITICAL):
• Shot on a 110 format pocket camera, the small cartridge-film format common for casual snapshots in the era
• Slightly soft, grainy, low-resolution image quality with a warm golden haze
• Simple tourist-snapshot framing, subject squarely centered
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity and period-accurate early-80s clothing. Mood: proud, a little starstruck, the classic 'I was there' photo.

name: STRATA SELF
message:
Take a picture and transform the subject into a vertical geological core sample — a cross-section of rock strata pulled from the earth, where each horizontal band represents a different era of the subject's life or a different age of the world, stacked from oldest at the bottom to newest at the top. Faint fossil-like impressions of the subject's face, hands, or silhouette should be visible embedded within certain strata bands, like a fossil record of a single person across deep time. Color and material should shift by band — sedimentary rust and ochre in older layers, ash-gray in a mid layer suggesting catastrophe, bright mineral veins near the top suggesting the present.

CRITICAL:
• This is a cross-section core sample, not a person standing next to rock
• The subject's recognizable face should appear at least once, clearly, in the topmost or most detailed band
• Include a measurement scale or depth markers along one edge, like a real geological core photograph
additionalInstructions: Preserve identity in the clearest band. Mood: awe at deep time, the strange comfort of being a small layer in something enormous.

name: ONE LIFE, ONE FRAME
message:
Take a picture and reimagine it as a single continuous unbroken scene — one hallway, one beach, one road, or one staircase — along which the subject appears multiple times simultaneously at different ages, walking the same path from infancy to old age, all coexisting in the same unified light and environment. The youngest version should be furthest in the background or at one end, the oldest nearest the foreground or at the other end, with two or three ages in between, all clearly the same recognizable person.

CRITICAL:
• All age-versions occupy ONE continuous physical space — no panels, no grid, no side-by-side comparison layout
• Consistent lighting and perspective across every age so it reads as one real photograph, not a collage
• Each version should be doing something small and human — glancing back, reaching a hand out, pausing — that visually links them
additionalInstructions: Preserve facial identity across all ages using consistent bone structure. Mood: tender, vertiginous, a whole life seen at once.

name: THE UNRAVELING
message:
Take a picture and transform it into the moment a person begins to vanish from their own history. Render the subject partially translucent, edges dissolving into faint light particles or fading like an old photograph left in the sun, starting from the extremities inward. Other people or elements in the frame should be behaving completely normally, unaware anything is wrong — the fading is only visible to the viewer. If the setting allows, include a framed photograph or mirror within the scene where the fading is even further along, as evidence of an unraveling timeline.

CRITICAL:
• The subject is disappearing FROM existence, not being erased digitally — this should read as a physical, photographic phenomenon happening in real time
• Surrounding people/environment remain fully solid and ordinary
• Do not make this a horror or gore scene — the tone is quiet dread and urgency, not violence
additionalInstructions: Preserve enough of the subject's features that they're still clearly recognizable despite the fading. Mood: urgent, eerie, a race against a clock no one else can see.

name: TEMPORAL STORM
message:
Take a picture and place the subject caught in a violent storm made entirely of time itself, rather than water or wind. Instead of rain, vintage photographs and torn calendar pages fall from a churning sky. Instead of hail, spinning brass pocket-watch gears and clock hands pelt the ground. A distant funnel cloud is built from a spiraling column of newspaper headlines spanning decades, and lightning flashes strobe like old film sprockets rather than ordinary bolts. The subject shields themselves or stands defiant against the chaos, hair and clothing whipped by the temporal wind.

CRITICAL:
• The storm's debris must clearly read as objects related to time and memory — photographs, clocks, newsprint, film — not generic debris
• Ground and sky should feel real and physically grounded despite the surreal storm content, like a genuine weather photograph of an impossible event

options.text: Hailing clock gears and pocket watches

additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity. Mood: exhilarating, chaotic, a little frightening — weather that shouldn't exist.

name: MUSEUM VITRINE, YEAR 2500
message:
Take a picture and transform it into a museum exhibit centuries in the future, where the subject and an ordinary modern object they're holding (phone, coffee cup, backpack, etc.) are displayed behind glass as a preserved historical relic. The vitrine sits in a sleek, unfamiliar future museum with soft ambient lighting, and one or two future visitors in unfamiliar advanced clothing lean in with curious expressions. A placard beside the display gives the subject and object a formal-sounding but confidently WRONG interpretation of what they were used for, written in the dry, authoritative tone of real museum placards.

CRITICAL:
• The placard text must be short, legible, and genuinely humorous through its wrongness
• Future visitors and architecture should look plausibly advanced but not identical to any specific existing sci-fi franchise
• The subject inside the vitrine should be rendered as a lifelike preserved figure, dignified rather than mocked
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity clearly through the glass. Mood: funny, a little humbling, gently absurd.

name: TIME MACHINE COCKPIT
message:
Take a picture and place the subject at the controls inside a time machine mid-jump, gripping brass-and-glass levers on a dense instrument panel crowded with spinning year-dials that can't agree on a number. Outside the cockpit windows, the view doesn't show empty space — it shows overlapping flashes of multiple eras streaking past simultaneously (a torch-lit medieval street, a neon future skyline, a dust-bowl prairie) blurred together like a long exposure. Electric-blue temporal energy crackles along exposed wiring and control housings, and the subject's hair or clothing reacts to the turbulence of the jump.

CRITICAL:
• The cockpit should feel handmade and mechanical, not a sleek modern spaceship — brass, copper, exposed gears, warm indicator bulbs
• The view through the windows must show multiple distinct eras bleeding into each other, not a single sci-fi environment
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity. Mood: thrilling, disorienting, the exact second before arrival.

name: SAME SPOT, FOUR CENTURIES
message:
Take a picture and reimagine the exact location as a single frame where four distinct centuries of that same spot are all visible at once, bleeding into each other like layered double exposures sharing the same architectural bones. A horse-drawn-era version of the street should ghost through a mid-20th-century version, which ghosts through a neon-future version, all anchored to the same fixed points (a doorway, a lamppost, a window) so the eye can track how the location changed. The subject stands in the present-day layer, solid and in focus, while the other eras are progressively more translucent around them.

CRITICAL:
• Anchor points (a specific doorway, corner, or landmark) must remain structurally recognizable across all four eras so the layering reads as ONE place across time, not four unrelated scenes
• Subject is the only fully solid, non-transparent element in the frame
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity. Mood: haunting, historical, a place remembering everything that ever happened in it.

name: RETROCAUSALITY
message:
Take a picture and depict an impossible moment where cause and effect are running backward. Choose one clear physical event and render it mid-reversal: shattered glass fragments floating together back into a whole pane, spilled liquid rising off the ground back into its glass, smoke pulling inward toward its source instead of dispersing, or footprints un-forming behind the subject as they walk. The subject should be the one calm, ordinary element in the frame, reacting with mild curiosity rather than alarm, as if this is simply what happens around them.

CRITICAL:
• Only ONE reversed physical event per image — do not combine multiple reversed phenomena, which reads as chaotic rather than eerie
• Everything else in the scene (lighting, subject, background) should behave completely normally, so the single reversed element stands out clearly

options.text: Spilled liquid rising back into its glass
Smoke pulling backward into its source

additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity. Mood: quiet, uncanny, a small tear in the arrow of time.

name: THE QUIET WITNESS
message:
Take a picture and place the subject, exactly as they appear now in their own modern clothing, standing calmly in an authentic prehistoric landscape — a Cretaceous floodplain with distant dinosaurs, an Ice Age tundra at dusk, or the ash-lit sky of a deep-time volcanic event. The subject is not costumed, not hiding, not intervening — simply present, an impossible anachronism captured in an otherwise completely believable, documentary-style prehistoric photograph, calmly observing rather than reacting with fear or urgency.

CRITICAL:
• The environment and prehistoric life must be rendered with scientific, documentary realism, not cartoonish
• The subject's calm, ordinary presence — not alarm or action — is the entire point; this is quiet impossibility, not an adventure scene
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity and their real, ordinary clothing exactly as photographed. Mood: still, contemplative, deep time with a single human-shaped exception.

name: YEAR ZERO
message:
Take a picture and place the subject beneath an enormous glowing countdown display dominating the sky or built into the architecture around them, its massive digits ticking down toward zero. At the frame's edges, reality should visibly begin to fray and dissolve into light and static, as if the world itself is holding its breath for whatever the countdown reaches. The subject's expression and posture should be genuinely ambiguous — this could be the final second before an ending, or the final second before something entirely new begins — and the image should not resolve that ambiguity.

CRITICAL:
• The countdown digits must be large, legible, and clearly approaching zero (single digits remaining)
• Fraying/dissolving reality should be confined to the frame's edges, leaving the subject and the countdown itself the clearest, most stable elements
additionalInstructions: Preserve subject identity clearly. Mood: deliberately ambiguous — equal parts dread and hope, ending and beginning.
